title: Proven Winners Just Launched Houseplants Sorted by Room, Not Species — Here's What Actually Fits an Apartment
intro: Proven Winners, the wholesale plant brand best known for supplying big-box garden centers, has partnered with The Plant Company to roll out leafjoy — a houseplant program that's organized differently than a normal nursery aisle. Instead of grouping plants by genus, leafjoy sorts its roughly 107 varieties into four collections by the actual room conditions they're bred to handle: Atrium (bright light), Cocoon (low light, north- or east-facing rooms with small windows), SpaScene (humid bathrooms and laundry rooms), and WorkLife (compact, space-saving plants for desks and tabletops). It's rolling out now at Home Depot, independent garden centers, and directly through leafjoystore.com and GrowJoy, with individual plants running roughly $25-$31 depending on size and pot. For apartment growers, the room-first sorting is the actual news here — it saves you the usual guesswork of buying a plant for its looks and then discovering it needs a south-facing window you don't have.

sections.heading: If your apartment's only bright spot is a north- or east-facing window, look at Cocoon
sections.body: Cocoon is leafjoy's collection built specifically for what the brand calls 'homebody' plants — ones that tolerate the lower light levels typical of interior rooms or small windows, and are explicitly marketed for north- or east-facing rooms rather than the bright south- or west-facing exposure most houseplant care tags assume you have. Two varieties in the lineup stand out for apartments: BeautiFall Golden Glen, a pothos with finer, more intricate chartreuse-and-lime variegation than a standard Hawaiian pothos, and Say Grace Maranta (prayer plant), which folds its leaves at night and tolerates the kind of indirect, low light a lot of apartment living rooms actually get. Both are sold as already-potted, mature plants rather than starter cuttings, so you're not waiting months to see the variegation or leaf pattern that sold you on it.

sections.heading: For a desk, nightstand, or dorm-sized surface, WorkLife is the collection to search first
sections.body: leafjoy's WorkLife collection is explicitly pitched as space-saving and vertical rather than sprawling, meant for desks and tabletops in home offices or dorm rooms — which maps directly onto the apartment problem of wanting greenery without giving up counter or desk space. The lineup includes compact Peperomia varieties like 'Sweet & Sour' and 'Spice is Nice', plus a Hoya 'Freckled Splash' wax vine with large, almond-shaped leaves that stays manageable in a small pot far longer than a full-size hoya. Peperomias in particular are a reasonable pick if you've killed pothos or philodendron from overwatering before — they store water in thick leaves and are more forgiving of an irregular watering schedule than most trailing vines.

sections.heading: If you travel or just forget to water, the H2O Mini line skips soil entirely
sections.body: leafjoy's H2O Mini collection is a hydroponic bottle-garden format — the plant sits in a water reservoir with roots visible through glass, and the brand's own care guidance is monthly watering or topping off once the vessel runs low, not a weekly schedule. That's a real fit for the specific apartment failure mode of forgetting a plant on a shelf for two weeks and finding it either bone-dry or root-rotted; a sealed water reservoir removes both failure modes at once, and the brand markets these for windowsills, desks, nightstands, bathrooms, and kitchens interchangeably since they don't need repotting or soil moisture checks. A leafjoy H2O Mini Aglaonema in a glass vase runs about $31 at Home Depot, which is genuinely pricier than a soil-potted plant of similar size, but you're paying for the container and the no-soil-maintenance format, not just the plant.

products.priceNote: Around $31 at Home Depot for the Aglaonema Pink Hybrid variety; other varieties in the H2O Mini line are similarly priced.

conclusion: The useful part of leafjoy isn't that it's a new brand — it's that the room-based sorting (Atrium/Cocoon/SpaScene/WorkLife) answers the question apartment growers actually have, which is 'what will survive in the specific light I've got,' before you fall for a plant's looks and find out later it needed a window you don't have. If you're working with a dim interior room, start with Cocoon; if it's desk or nightstand space you're short on, WorkLife's compact varieties are built for that footprint; and if your real constraint is your own inconsistent watering, the H2O Mini format trades a higher price tag for removing that variable almost entirely.
